---
title: "Overview of the IRW Data Standards"
---

Data standards are an essential mechanism of increasing reusability and interoperability of data amongst researchers. As such, they play a critical role in increasing the extent to which science is [FAIR](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201618) (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable). The IRW's response data come in several *data families* that use distinct data standards. We focus here on describing the families and the differences between their standards (with pointers to complete descriptions of the specific standards).

## The data families {#families}

Every response table in the IRW belongs to exactly one **data family**, and each family is kept in its own Redivis dataset. In the `irw` packages, the `source` argument selects the family.

| Family | `source =` | What defines it |
|---|---|---|
| Core | `"core"` (the default) | A person responds to an item; the responses are ordered or continuous |
| Nominal | `"nom"` | As in core, but the response categories have no order |
| Competitions | `"comp"` | Two entities meet and an outcome is recorded: a game, or a choice between two fixed things such as two essays |
| Simulated and synthetic | `"sim"` | Responses that no real person produced |
| Conjoint | `"conj"` | Respondents choose between, or rate, profiles whose attributes are assigned at random |

Four families are defined by the shape of the data. Simsyn is defined by where the data come from: a simulated table can have any shape, and it belongs to simsyn rather than to the family its shape would suggest.

### Core, competitions and conjoint

Set simsyn aside, and fold nominal into core (it differs only in that the response categories are unordered). That leaves three shapes of data. What separates them is what gets compared, and what we would want a parameter for.

- **Core.** A person responds to an item. Persons and items are categorically different things, and both persist: the same item is answered by many people. The usual model gives each of them a parameter, an ability and a difficulty, say.
- **Competitions.** There is no item. Two entities meet—teams in a game, chess engines, two essays put in front of a judge, two named options put to a voter—and an outcome is recorded. The entities recur across many comparisons, and the target is a parameter for each of them (an Elo rating, a Bradley–Terry strength). Where there is a judge, the judge is the instrument rather than the object of measurement.
- **Conjoint.** A person chooses between, or rates, profiles (hypothetical candidates, immigrants, policies) whose attributes are assigned at random. A profile is built for one task and never seen again, so there is nothing to give a parameter to. The target is instead the effect of each attribute on the response, and how that effect varies across people. In IRT terms, this sits closest to an explanatory model such as the LLTM, wherein the items are generated on the fly from their features.

A simple test sorts most new datasets. Do the things being responded to keep a stable identity, and would we want a parameter for each? If so, the data are core when a person responds to them one at a time and competitions when they are pitted against each other in pairs. If instead the things are assembled fresh from attributes and the question is which attributes drive the response, the data are conjoint. Note that a "conjoint" study that shows everyone the same fixed set of profiles fails the test: its profiles have identities, so it belongs in core or competitions.

Item text and the metadata are not families. They hold no responses and describe the tables in the families.

## The data standards

In all cases, we are interested in cross-classified responses. The differences amongst the standards pertain to the nature of either the cross-classification or the response.
